newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka troops capture key northern highway.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka troops capture key northern highway.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops captured a key highway linking two army-controlled towns in the island's north, completing the year's biggest offensive against separatist Tamil guerrillas, a military spokesman said on Saturday.
Troops, backed by artillery, tanks and air cover, linked up with troops at Mannar, an army-controlled coastal town 240 km (150 miles) north of the capital Colombo, he said.

The military, which launched its latest offensive code-named "Edi Bala" (brave force) on February 4 from Vavuniya, a government stronghold 220 km (140 miles) northeast of Colombo, advanced virtually unopposed in a westerly direction.
"The road from Vavuniya to Mannar is now open," the spokesman told Reuters.
Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte, accompanied by senior military officials, made the inaugural 80-km (50-mile) journey between the two towns on Friday, military officials in the area said.
The army's aim is to fortify its gains along the route and restrict the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) to areas north of the highway, the spokesman said.

The LTTE, fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in this predominantly Sinhalese Indian Ocean island's north and east, earlier controlled a large expanse of land south and southwest of the road.
The spokesman said the military would now be able to open an overland supply route to Mannar.
Mannar and the island of Talaimannar north of the town are controlled by the army while the surrounding areas are controlled by the rebels. Mannar was accessible to troops only by sea.

The LTTE's international spokesmen in London and Paris were not immediately available for comment, but a rebel statement faxed to Reuters late on Friday said the offensive had sent thousands of Tamil civilians fleeing from their homes.
"In this military offensive, like all others, Sri Lankan troops have been bulldozing their way through Tamil territory without regard for civilian casualties," the statement said.
It said Tamils had been forced to flee to India "as a last resort to escape the army advance".
Late on Wednesday, a fishing trawler carrying 150 Tamil refugees to India capsized in the Mannar sea, killing at least 130 people, mostly women and children, the statement said.
It asked all Tamils to observe a day of mourning on Saturday as a mark of respect for the people who were "trying to make it to India before Sri Lankan troops could arrive".
But the military denied the refugees were fleeing advancing troops.

"There were no large scale firefights in this offensive. There was no reason for civilians to flee," the spokesman said. "The LTTE has always been ferrying people to India. It has nothing to do with this offensive."
The Ministry of Defence said only five rebels were killed in the entire offensive, which was launched in two phases. There were no civilian or army casualties reported.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war, now in its 14th year. The LTTE says the toll is much higher.
